content: Verbascum thapsus, commonly known as Great Mullein or Common Mullein, is a biennial plant native to Europe, northern Africa, and Asia, but it has been introduced to the Americas and Australia. It is characterized by its tall, unbranched stems that can grow over 2 meters in height, and its small, densely packed yellow flowers. The plant forms a rosette of large, woolly leaves in its first year, and in its second year, it produces a flowering stem. The leaves are covered with silvery, star-shaped trichomes, and their size and shape vary along the stem. The flowers are pentamerous, with five stamens of two distinct types, and they produce small, ovoid seed capsules containing numerous minute seeds. This species thrives in well-lit, disturbed soils and is often found in sandy or chalky environments. It is not highly competitive and cannot tolerate shade, which limits its invasiveness. However, its seeds are long-lived, remaining viable in the soil for decades, and the plant can rapidly colonize bare ground, especially after disturbances like forest fires. Germination typically occurs in spring or summer when seeds are exposed to light, and the plant's life cycle is biennial, although some individuals may flower in their first or third year depending on environmental conditions. Great Mullein has a wide native range, extending from Europe and northern Africa to Asia, including regions such as the British Isles, Scandinavia, Siberia, and the Himalayas. It has been introduced to temperate regions worldwide, including North America, Australia, and New Zealand. In the United States, it was introduced in the 18th century for its medicinal and piscicidal properties and has since become widespread. The plant has been used medicinally for centuries, particularly for its emollient and astringent properties. It is commonly employed in the treatment of respiratory conditions such as coughs, bronchitis, and sore throats. The leaves and flowers contain mucilage, saponins, and glycosides, which contribute to its expectorant and soothing effects. Preparations of the plant, such as teas and decoctions, are used for pulmonary ailments, while topical applications are recommended for skin conditions like warts, boils, and eczema. The flowers also yield an oil used for earaches and other external conditions. Recent studies have identified glycyrrhizin compounds in the plant with bactericidal and potential anti-tumor properties. In addition to its medicinal uses, Great Mullein has been employed for various non-medical purposes. The seeds, which contain rotenone and other compounds, have been used as a piscicide. The flowers produce dyes in shades of yellow and green, and the dried leaves and stems have been used for making candle wicks and torches. The plant has also been associated with folklore, believed to ward off evil spirits and curses. Ecologically, Great Mullein serves as a host for numerous insects, including both pests and beneficial species. It is a potential reservoir for pests like thrips and spider mites, as well as diseases such as cucumber mosaic virus and powdery mildew. However, it also supports predatory insects that can aid in biological pest control. Control of the plant, when necessary, is best achieved through mechanical means such as hand-pulling or hoeing, as its hairy leaves make it resistant to grazing and some herbicides. Taxonomically, Verbascum thapsus was first described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753. It belongs to the section Bothrosperma, subsection Fasciculata, within the genus Verbascum. The species exhibits significant phenotypic variation in its native range, leading to numerous synonyms and subspecies classifications. Three recognized subspecies include V. thapsus subsp. thapsus, V. thapsus subsp. crassifolium, and V. thapsus subsp. giganteum, each with distinct morphological traits and geographic distributions. The plant is also known to hybridize with other Verbascum species. Common names for Great Mullein vary widely and often reference its appearance or texture, such as Woolly Mullein, Velvet Mullein, and Aaron's Rod. In North America, it is typically called Common Mullein. Historically, it has been known by numerous whimsical names, reflecting its widespread recognition and use.
